title: The Black Ledger
premise: The number in the courier's case is an entry in a book that Silas Vane keeps behind the one he shows people. For six years he has taken Blackstone silver to keep the valley's roads slow and its towns apart. The present rail attacks, held grain, chained mine and road interception are separate commissions within that network; each recipient has purposes of their own. He says he has kept four armies out of the valley with a pencil. He may be right. The town finds out before the stranger has decided, and comes to his porch with a rope, and Pritchard stands on the steps with a hand that will not hold still.

places.name: Vane's trading post
places.what: The best-stocked counter in the valleys, with a porch the whole town can see

places.name: The counting room
places.what: Behind the post: a high desk, a letter-press, and a safe from a bank that no longer has a town round it

places.name: The freight platform
places.what: Where the night freight sets down sealed crates, and Beckett signs for them in a glove

places.name: Vane's porch
places.what: Six steps up from the street. Room for two people to stand at the top and a crowd at the bottom

stages.set_by: Pritchard naming Vane's book, after The Four Flags completes
stages.log: The number is a page in a book of Silas Vane's that nobody has seen. Pritchard can ask for it with a warrant. He would rather somebody else looked first.

stages.set_by: Walking into the counting room beside Pritchard with his warrant
stages.log: Pritchard put the warrant on Vane's counter and did not sit down when he was asked.

stages.set_by: Opening the safe during the Harvest Supper, while Vane is carving
stages.log: The whole town is at Vane's table. His safe was not hard, for somebody who knew he was born in the year of the flood.

stages.set_by: Taking the strongbox from Beckett on the freight platform, by force or by the night freight's lantern code
stages.log: You have the box that came off the night freight, and what was in it: silver, and the month's page for the book.

stages.set_by: Vane's button, offered only to a stranger the valley has reason to distrust
stages.log: Silas Vane opened the book himself and turned it round on the desk. He said he had been waiting six years for somebody with the stomach to read it.
Four columns. Rail. River. Mine. Road. A payment against each. And a fifth column, received, with a small square drawn where a name should be.

stages.set_by: Beckett stepping between the player and the door with the box open
stages.log: Temperance Beckett has a sawn-off in a cash box and has corrected your arithmetic. She says the book stays.
Temperance Beckett died in the counting room doorway with the ledger-box still under her arm.

stages.set_by: The button 'He left you everything, and himself nothing.'
stages.log: Temperance Beckett put the box down on the desk, very carefully, and went and stood by the window.

stages.set_by: The crowd reaching the porch, at dusk on the day the book is read
stages.log: The town is in the street with a rope. Pritchard is on the porch steps with his hand in his coat. Silas Vane has put on a clean collar.

stages.set_by: The button '(Read the book out from the porch)'
stages.log: You read it out, page by page, to the whole street. Nobody shouted. That was worse.

stages.set_by: The button 'Sign it over, and they never hear the rest.'
stages.log: Silas Vane signed away the holds on rail, river and mine with the town at his door. The street was told there had been a mistake in the accounts.

stages.set_by: The button 'You work for me now.'
stages.log: Silas Vane keeps his counter and his pencil. He keeps them for you. He says it is the first honest contract he has signed in six years.

stages.set_by: Only the explicit informed choice after the player has arrived and heard the rope warning. Closing a menu, leaving to think or never visiting the porch is not this choice.
stages.log: They hanged Silas Vane from his own sign-bracket. Owen Pritchard did not draw. He has not been seen out of his office since.

stages.set_by: Learning where the silver comes from: from Vane, from Beckett, from the book's last page or from Haskell's hidden weight-sheet
stages.log: The silver comes down on the night freight from Blackstone Station. Nobody in the valley has been up that line in six years. Somebody up there has been paying for the quiet.

objectives.text: Get a look at the book Silas Vane does not show
The town is at Vane's porch. Get there
Find out where the silver comes from

options.label: Bring your warrant, Sheriff.
options.now: In by the front door in daylight with Pritchard beside you
options.later: It is lawful and the town knows by noon. Pritchard has to watch his friend's face while you read

options.label: (Go in during the Harvest Supper)
options.now: The safe, by candle, while the whole town eats at Vane's table
options.later: Nobody knows you have read it. What you do next is yours alone

options.label: (Meet the night freight)
options.now: Take the month's box from Beckett on the platform
options.later: You have silver in your hands and Beckett at your back. Vane knows before breakfast

options.label: I hear you keep two books.
options.now: Ask him. If the valley has cause to distrust you, he shows you himself
options.later: He believes you are his kind. Everything after starts from that

options.label: (Read the book out from the porch)
options.now: The street hears all of it and goes home
options.later: Vane lives, ruined. Credit stops at every counter in the valleys for a month. Every flag at the fair sends a man with an offer

options.label: Sign it over, and they never hear the rest.
options.now: The holds are lifted tonight. The town is told it was an error
options.later: Rail, river and mine open by spring. Those who buried somebody this year are never told why. It is yours to keep quiet

options.label: You work for me now.
options.now: Vane stays at his counter under your hand
options.later: You own the best ledger in the valleys and the man who can read the fifth column. The town has been lied to twice

options.label: Let the crowd hang him.
options.later: The book burns with the post. Pritchard is finished. Whoever sent the silver sends it to someone else

evidence.found: The safe in the counting room; or the month's page in the box off the night freight
Folded inside the lining of the receiving book at Haskell's desk; he hands it over if asked a direct question
Beckett, if she lives: the hand that passes the box out of the car wears a glove with a square mark on the cuff
In the safe, under the book

ways_through: Go in with Pritchard's warrant, read the book, stand on the porch and step aside or speak. Needs nothing from any earlier road and nothing optional.
Burgle the safe during the supper and decide alone what the town learns.
Take the box from the night freight and work back from the silver.
Be shown the book by Vane and take his offer or turn it on him.
cannot_break: If Vane is killed before the book is read, the book is still in the safe and Beckett holds the room. If Beckett is killed, Haskell's weight-sheet names the station. If both are dead the last page of the book has the square mark and a freight number, and the yard at Iron Junction can say which platform it leaves from. No offscreen automatic lynching when the player fails to arrive. The threatened confrontation remains unresolved. Main Blackstone evidence may still be learned through the existing Vane/Beckett/book/Haskell alternatives; no porch choice may be secretly assigned just to complete the chapter. If Pritchard is absent, Talbot stands on the steps, or nobody does. The side quest is not needed: a stranger who sold Vane the Line 14 book only finds it lying open on his desk.

open_questions: Resolved 2026-11-16: one purse, independent hands. Vane funds the network; he does not control every hand or know the explanation (decision 1).
Resolved by packet 2: the hanging happens only by the explicit, warned choice. Leaving, closing the box or never coming to the porch does not choose it.
Resolved by packet 3: Pritchard's reply names the choice and his own responsibility, and is said only by a living Pritchard.
